t: LeetCode 3357 — Minimize the Maximum Adjacent Element Difference
o: We replace every -1 with either x or y (one global pair, chosen once) so that the largest absolute difference between neighbors is as small as possible. The answer is monotone: if difference d is achievable, any d' > d is too, which invites a binary search on the answer. For a fixed d, only three things matter: (1) adjacent pairs of known values must already differ by at most d — this is a hard lower bound; (2) every known value sitting next to a -1 (call these *critical* values) must lie within d of x or within d of y; (3) runs of consecutive -1s impose no extra constraint since we can fill them with equal values. In Example 1 the critical values are {2, 10, 8}; picking (6,7) puts each within 4 of one of the two picks, giving answer 4. In Example 3 the critical values {10, 8} sit within 1 of 11 and 9 respectively. With n up to 1e5 and values up to 1e9, we need roughly O(n log V): binary search over d with a fast feasibility test.
k: The answer is monotone in d, so binary search on the maximum allowed difference.
For a fixed d, only known values adjacent to a -1 matter; adjacent known-known pairs give a hard lower bound on d.
Covering sorted critical values with two intervals of length 2d can be done greedily: start the first interval at the smallest value, and the second at the first uncovered value.
The greedy check collapses to an O(1) test per step: it suffices that no critical value lies strictly between minV + 2d and maxV - 2d.

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search on the answer + greedy interval covering
a.i: Binary search on d. Feasibility for a given d reduces to covering all critical values with the two intervals [x-d, x+d] and [y-d, y+d]. Sorting the critical values and greedily placing the first interval at the leftmost uncovered point is optimal for covering points with fixed-length intervals, so two intervals suffice exactly when the greedy uses at most two. The lower bound of the search is the maximum difference among adjacent known-known pairs, since that constraint cannot be changed by filling.
s: Scan nums: record base = max |difference| over adjacent known-known pairs; collect every known value whose neighbor is -1 into a list crit.
If crit is empty, return base immediately.
Sort crit. Define feasible(d): greedily sweep with at most two intervals of radius d — repeatedly take the smallest uncovered value v, skip all values <= v + 2d; succeed if nothing remains.
Binary search the smallest d in [base, max(crit) - min(crit)] for which feasible(d) holds.
a.t: O(n log n + n log V) — sorting the critical values plus ~31 binary-search iterations, each doing a linear greedy sweep.
a.sp: O(n) — the list of critical values.

a.n: Approach 2: Binary search with an O(1) min/max feasibility test (optimal)
a.i: The greedy covering test can be simplified dramatically. In an optimal covering, the left interval should be placed as far right as possible while still covering the minimum critical value mn, i.e. at center mn + d (covering up to mn + 2d); symmetrically the right interval covers down to mx - 2d where mx is the maximum. Moving intervals this way never loses coverage of anything an optimal solution covered, so d is feasible iff every critical value v satisfies v <= mn + 2d or v >= mx - 2d — i.e., no critical value lies strictly inside (mn + 2d, mx - 2d). This removes sorting entirely.
s: Scan nums once: track base = max adjacent known-known difference and the min mn / max mx over known values adjacent to a -1.
If no such values exist, return base.
Define feasible(d): false iff some critical value v has mn + 2d < v < mx - 2d (checked in O(1) via the tracked extremes by re-scanning or storing values).
Binary search the smallest feasible d starting from base.
a.t: O(n log V) — about 31 binary-search iterations over the value range, each with an O(n) scan; no sorting needed.
a.sp: O(n) — stored critical values (can be reduced to O(1) extra by tracking mn, mx and re-scanning nums per check).

w: In an interview, present Approach 1 first (binary search + greedy covering is easy to argue), then mention the min/max simplification of Approach 2 as the polished solution. Common pitfalls: forgetting the hard lower bound from adjacent known-known pairs (binary search must start there, otherwise you may return a smaller infeasible value); treating a run of consecutive -1s as requiring |x - y| <= d (it does not — fill the run with one repeated value); double-counting a known value with two missing neighbors (harmless if collected into a set-like check, but keep the scan simple); and overflow when computing 2*d with values up to 1e9 in C++/Java (use 64-bit). Edge cases: all elements -1 (answer 0), no missing elements (answer is the max adjacent difference), and missing elements only at the ends. Follow-ups: solve without binary search in O(n) by deriving the answer directly from the largest known-known gap and the extreme critical values, or handle k distinct replacement values instead of two.
